one_line: A flat gas burner on the Space Station imitated small burning patches of plastics and liquids in still air, showing that such flames can burn steadily for minutes without any air flow when oxygen is raised to about 26.5% or more, but go out within tens of seconds at 21%.
summary: ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) used flat porous gas burners, 25 and 50 mm across, in the Combustion Integrated Rack on the International Space Station to imitate small burning patches of solids and liquids in still air. Ethylene, nitrogen-diluted ethylene or methane was fed at a fixed mass flux (about 1-12 g/(m2 s)) into nitrogen-oxygen atmospheres of 21-40% O2 at 56-100 kPa; embedded heat-flux gauges, radiometers and cameras gave the effective heat of gasification of each flame, its radiative loss and its size. Over 18 test days in 2019-2021, 194 flames were ignited. All 25 mm flames at 21% O2 self-extinguished within 40 s, whereas at 26.5, 34 and 40% O2 many burned steadily for 2-5 minutes until shut down. Larger, higher-flow and methane flames extinguished sooner; radiative heat loss drove the oscillation and extinction. Models built on these data suggest common plastics could burn steadily at about 1-3 g/(m2 s) in microgravity, and that low-pressure, oxygen-enriched cabin atmospheres widen the burning range. Stopping ventilation may therefore not quickly put out a small fire at elevated oxygen.

question.text: Can a small condensed-fuel (solid or liquid) fire burn steadily in quiescent microgravity, where there is no buoyant or forced flow to bring oxygen in, and if so for which combinations of material properties and cabin atmospheres? Testing dozens of real materials in orbit is too expensive, so BRE emulates them: a porous gas burner fed with ethylene or methane (optionally diluted with nitrogen) is set to match a material's heat of combustion, heat of gasification, surface re-radiation and smoke point. The hypothesis is that a quasi-steady burning regime exists as a function of these properties, and that if so the ground-based cone calorimeter test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 2), which measures such properties, could be used to build microgravity flammability maps for real materials. Objectives also named three NASA-considered cabin atmospheres (21% O2 at 14.7 psia, 26.5% at 10.2 psia, 34% at 8.2 psia), O2/CO2 ambients (desired) and extinction limits.

sources.quote: Ground-based tests are too short to overcome ignition transients and testing dozens of condensed fuels in orbit is prohibitively expensive.
In this fire safety study, the flammability of solid and liquid materials is simulated by burning gaseous fuels under key conditions corresponding to the solid and liquid materials.

physics.text: On Earth a burning surface is fed by a buoyant plume that brings in fresh air and carries away hot products. In quiescent microgravity there is no buoyancy, so oxygen reaches the flame only by diffusion; the flame becomes a slowly growing, nominally hemispherical blue diffusion flame over the surface. For a steadily burning condensed fuel the mass burning rate equals the net heat flux to the surface divided by the heat of gasification L (energy needed to turn unit mass of solid or liquid into vapour), so L = q''_net / m''. BRE inverts this: the fuel mass flux m'' is imposed through the porous burner, the heat flux to the surface is measured, and the 'effective' L of the emulated material is derived. Stagnant-layer (Spalding B-number) theory gives a purely diffusive burning rate proportional to ln(1+B). Because microgravity flames are large, slow and long-lived, radiative loss from soot and from CO2/H2O becomes a large fraction of the heat release; as the flame grows the flame temperature drops until it oscillates and undergoes radiative extinction. Higher oxygen raises flame temperature; dilution with nitrogen lowers heat of combustion and makes flames smaller and less radiative. A drop-tower test (5 s) is too short for these flames to reach steady state, hence the need for ISS-duration tests.

sources.note: Diffusion-limited quiescent burning, B-number theory and radiative extinction of microgravity diffusion flames are textbook combustion background.

equations.latex: L = \frac{\dot q''_{net}}{\dot m''}, \qquad \dot q''_{net} = \dot q''_{f,c} + \dot q''_{f,r} - \dot q''_{s,r} + \dot q''_{e,r}
equations.meaning: Steady energy balance at a burning surface, used by BRE to define the emulated material. $L$: heat of gasification (kJ/g), energy to turn unit mass of condensed fuel into vapour at the surface; $\dot q''_{net}$: net heat flux into the surface (kW/m2), measured by the burner's heat-flux gauges and slug calorimeter; $\dot m''$: fuel mass flux (g/(m2 s)), imposed through the porous burner. Components: flame convective flux $\dot q''_{f,c}$, flame radiative flux $\dot q''_{f,r}$, surface re-radiation $\dot q''_{s,r}$ and external radiation $\dot q''_{e,r}$ (zero in the ISS tests). Exact for a simply vaporising fuel at steady state; only approximate for real pyrolysis (charring, in-depth heating).

sources.quote: burning of a condensed fuel, the heat of gasification L is given by the ratio of the net heat flux and the burning rate.
the heat of gasification, L, (a material property) is found by Eq. (4.8)
The external radiative heat flux is not present in the experiments but could be included in the theory to follow.
This is exact for vaporizing solids and approximant under real pyrolysis conditions.

equations.latex: B = \frac{Y_{O_2,\infty}(1 - X_r)\,\Delta h_c / S - c_p (T_s - T_\infty)}{L_e}, \qquad L_e = L - \frac{\dot q''_{f,r} + \dot q''_{e,r} - \dot q''_{s,r}}{\dot m''}
equations.meaning: Spalding B number (mass transfer number): ratio of the energy the flame can deliver per unit mass of fuel to the energy needed to gasify it. $Y_{O_2,\infty}$: ambient O2 mass fraction; $\Delta h_c$: heat of combustion of the fuel/diluent stream (kJ/g; 15-47.2 kJ/g in BRE); $S$: mass of O2 consumed per unit mass of fuel stream; $\Delta h_c/S$ is the heat released per unit mass of O2 (taken as 13.76 kJ/g for ethylene); $c_p$: gas specific heat (kJ/(g K), consistent with $L$ and $\Delta h_c/S$); $T_s$, $T_\infty$: surface and ambient temperatures (K); $L$: heat of gasification (kJ/g); $L_e$: effective heat of gasification (kJ/g), $L$ less the net radiative fluxes per unit mass flux (dissertation Eq. 4.6 and 4.7), so that $\dot m'' L_e$ is the convective flux alone. The Dehghani analysis uses this effective B, in which the heat of combustion is reduced by the flame radiative loss fraction $X_r$ (transparent-flame assumption) and the denominator is $L_e$; $X_r$ and $L_e$ belong together. With $X_r = 0$ and no radiative fluxes this is the classical textbook B number. Higher O2 raises B and so the burning rate.

equations.latex: \dot m'' = \frac{8k}{\pi c_p D}\,\ln(1 + B) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \lambda \equiv \frac{\pi c_p R\,\dot m''}{4k} = \ln(1 + B)
equations.meaning: Steady, purely diffusive burning rate of a flat circular fuel surface in quiescent surroundings (stagnant-layer and oblate-ellipsoid models give the same form); the relation BRE is built on. $\dot m''$: fuel mass flux (kg/(m2 s)); $k$: gas thermal conductivity (W/(m K)); $c_p$: gas specific heat (J/(kg K)); $D = 2R$: burner diameter (m); $\lambda$: dimensionless mass flux (burning eigenvalue); $B$: Spalding B number. Unity Lewis number ($\rho\mathcal{D} = k/c_p$), constant properties, laminar, no buoyancy. Note the rate scales as $1/D$, so small surfaces burn faster per unit area. In BRE $\dot m''$ is prescribed, so the relation is inverted to find the $B$ (and hence $L$) a flame emulates. Neglecting radiation, it over-predicted the measured drop-tower burning rates, and the 25 and 50 mm data followed two distinct curves.

equations.meaning: Flame temperature of the steady flame with radiative loss, and the extinction criterion the investigators used. $T_f$: flame temperature (K); $Y_{F,s}$: fuel mass fraction at the surface; $X_r$: flame radiative loss fraction; other symbols as above. A flame is predicted to burn steadily only if $T_f$ exceeds a critical value of about 1100 K, the value commonly used for low-strain (about 1 s$^{-1}$) microgravity flames, versus about 1600 K for buoyant 1-g flames (strain about 10 s$^{-1}$). apparatus.text: Flat, round, porous gas burners of 25 mm and 50 mm diameter with a copper top plate, embedded heat-flux gauges (two on the 25 mm burner: centre and offset at 9.5 mm radius), a copper slug calorimeter and surface thermocouples, mounted in the ACME chamber insert inside the CIR combustion chamber (nominally ~100 L, about 15 L occupied by hardware). The insert provides a hot-wire igniter, mass flow controllers for fuel delivery, a radiometer array, photomultiplier tubes (one with an OH* filter) and cameras; tests are configured by ISS crew and commanded remotely from NASA Glenn.

procedure.text: For each test the crew/ground set the chamber atmosphere (diluent, O2 concentration, pressure), started fuel flow at a fixed rate and ignited it with the hot-wire igniter. The flame was observed at constant flow while burner surface temperature and heat flux evolved; a test ended either at self-extinction or, for flames that appeared steady, by commanded fuel shutdown (in practice after about 2-5 min, partly to conserve fuel and keep the atmosphere roughly constant). The planned extinction-limit procedure was to reduce flow stepwise after the burner reached steady temperature. Ignition limits were deliberately not studied in orbit. Several ignitions were made per test day: 194 flames over 18 test days, 2019-02-08 to 2021-01-28 (a 2019 round and a 2020-21 round after a one-year hiatus). Normal-gravity lab tests with gas, liquid and solid fuels, 5.18 s drop-tower tests at NASA Glenn and CFD modelling supported the flight work.

findings.claim: Oxygen threshold for the 25 mm ethylene/N2 flames tested: all flames in 21% O2 (by volume) self-extinguished within 40 s, whereas steady flames were observed at nominal 26.5%, 34% and 40% O2. NASA's summary places the self-extinction boundary at roughly 25% O2. This is a threshold for these burner conditions (flow rates, sizes), not a material flammability limit.

findings.claim: Mapping derived heats of gasification onto real materials suggests that, at 25 mm scale, polyethylene and polypropylene could burn steadily in microgravity at about 3 g/(m2 s), nylon and PMMA at about 2.5 g/(m2 s), and a phenolic-glass composite at about 1 g/(m2 s) - much lower rates than in 1 g (PMMA ~19 g/(m2 s) at 25 mm), implying materials may burn more easily but more slowly in microgravity. On the resulting flammability map an emulated PMMA flame falls in the flammable zone at X_O2 0.40 and 0.34 but in the extinction zone at 0.265. These are model-based inferences from emulator data, not tests of the materials.

findings.claim: Simulations of the ISS test conditions in normal air (3-D, transient) reproduce the observed time to extinction; extinction happens when the instantaneous radiative fraction rises to 60-70% of the current heat release rate, a level reached because the low-momentum microgravity flame has a long residence time. After local extinction the flame edge takes a hook-like (bibrachial) form, and on re-ignition a triple flame runs along the stoichiometric surface.

sources.quote: Time to flame extinction predicted in this work agrees with the experimental observations. Extinction occurs due to the excessive radiative losses when the instantaneous radiative fraction grows up to 60–70% of the current heat release rate.
The excessively high level of the radiative losses is facilitated by the long residence time in the low-momentum microgravity flame.

relevance.text: Spacecraft fire response relies partly on stopping ventilation to starve a fire. BRE indicates that a small burning surface can keep burning for minutes in still air in microgravity, particularly in oxygen-enriched atmospheres, so turning off flow may not extinguish a fire quickly at elevated O2. The investigators suggest NASA make more use of the cone-calorimeter-based flammability Test 2, whose measured properties (heat of combustion, heat of gasification) map onto BRE's flammability maps, alongside the upward-flame-spread Test 1. Transferability caveats: BRE is a gas burner with imposed fuel flow; it does not pyrolyse, melt, drip, char or spread, and L is derived as heat flux / mass flux, which is exact only for simply vaporising fuels. Emulation was validated for several materials in 1 g, but its accuracy for real materials in microgravity was not directly verified with real samples on ISS. Sizes were 25 and 50 mm only. The O2 thresholds therefore describe burner flames at the tested flow rates, not material flammability limits.

sources.quote: Significance: Spacecraft fire prevention, including (1) microgravity flammability conditions and (2) assessment of flammability test methods for spacecraft materials.
This is exact for vaporizing solids and approximant under real pyrolysis conditions.

This technique has been demonstrated for a wide variety of materials in normal-gravity and could provide an efficient way to screen and select fire-resistant materials for use in spacecraft, if the technique is similarly effective in microgravity.
Seven condensed fuels were emulated: acetone, ethanol, methanol, polyethylene, polymethylmethacrylate, polypropylene, and polystyrene.

habitat_conditions.text: The test atmospheres bracket the NASA-considered cabin atmospheres named in the objective: 21% O2 at 14.7 psia (101.4 kPa), 26.5% at 10.2 psia (70.3 kPa) and 34% at 8.2 psia (56.5 kPa, the exploration atmosphere). The dissertation describes these nominal pairs as 21% at 1 bar, 26.5% at 0.7 bar and 34% at 0.565 bar. Steady burning was seen at 26.5% and 34% (and at 40%, above any proposed habitat level), while 21% flames self-extinguished; i.e. the exploration atmosphere (34% O2, 56.5 kPa) falls on the side where these small flames persist. Pressures per test are not in PSI. Against the shared reference atmospheres: the 21% O2 / ~100 kPa tests correspond to Earth sea level (20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa), where these flames self-extinguished. The 34% O2 / 56.5 kPa case lies inside the Moon-habitat envelope (30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa or less), and the 40% tests exceed it in O2; the 26.5% / 70.3 kPa case is at the envelope's pressure but below its O2. Steady burning was observed in all three of these enriched conditions. Spacesuit conditions (100% O2 at 29.6 kPa) were far outside the tested range (at most 40% O2, at least ~56 kPa).

sources.quote: Three of the atmospheres are nominal NASA selected atmospheres of pressure and oxygen for human habitat in space flight: 21 % oxygen and 1 bar, 26.5% and 0.7 bar and 34 % and 0.565 bar
All flames burning in 21% by volume oxygen self-extinguished within 40 s. However, steady flames were observed at 26.5, 34, and 40% oxygen.
This is further support of the significant hazards of using enriched oxygen atmospheres in spacecraft.

earth_benefits.text: The emulation approach and its 1-g validation (wick and gas-burner tests on ignition and extinction of small fires) are aimed at fire science generally; NASA states the results could improve fire safety on Earth, but no specific Earth application is documented in the sources reached.

sources.quote: While BRE is focused on improving the process to select fire-resistant spacecraft materials, the research results could yield new understanding that also enables improved fire safety on Earth.

limitations.text: Emulation, not real materials: a gas burner with prescribed fuel flow cannot reproduce pyrolysis chemistry, charring, melting, bubbling, dripping, in-depth heating or flame spread; real-material burning in microgravity was not tested.

sources.quote: This is exact for vaporizing solids and approximant under real pyrolysis conditions.

sources.note: Physical difference between a fed gas burner and a pyrolysing solid.

limitations.text: Only 25 and 50 mm burners; results are size-dependent (larger flames radiated more and extinguished sooner), so extrapolation to larger fires is uncertain.

sources.quote: larger flames were generally seen to self-extinguish within 1.5 minutes.
It is shown that as burner diameter is increased, flame radiant fraction is increased, and heats of gasification are decreased.

limitations.text: Quiescent ambient only; no ventilation-flow cases, so results apply to post-ventilation-shutdown conditions, not to normal cabin airflow.
Only ethylene and methane (with N2) were used; heat of combustion range 15-47.2 kJ/g; smoke point is set by these fuels. Methane flames behaved differently (short-lived).

sources.quote: The resulting heats of combustion were 15 – 47.2 kJ/g.
methane flames were seen to self-extinguish within a minute.

limitations.text: Measurement issues: the slug calorimeter's operation was compromised and needed a theoretical correction; heat-flux gauges showed early water-condensation artefacts.

sources.quote: its operation was compromised, and a theoretical correction had to be imposed.
This is believed to be due to early water condensation on the gages from the combustion products in contact with a relatively cool sensor.

limitations.text: Steadiness is inferred from theory (flames were shut down at ~2-5 min to conserve fuel and keep the atmosphere constant), and the slowly varying chamber atmosphere during a day's tests is not documented in PSI.

sources.quote: This had to be done to conserve fuel and maintain reasonably constant atmospheres.

open_questions: PSI lacks per-test conditions; with the investigators' Table 3.1 (O2, fuel fraction, pressure, mass flux, heat fluxes, flame size, burn time, end point) one could build an O2-pressure-mass-flux map of steady vs self-extinguished outcomes.
Reconcile the 194 flames in the PSI table with the 149 successful ignitions reported in the dissertation (possibly different subsets, e.g. methane or 50 mm tests).
Analysis of the methane and 50 mm tests is only summarised in slides; quantitative extinction-time results for them were not found beyond the Wright thesis abstract.
Whether the O2/CO2 ambients (objective 2) and stepwise flow-reduction extinction tests (objective 3) were actually run is not documented in the sources reached.
Direct comparison of BRE-predicted flammability with cone-calorimeter (Test 2) data for specific spacecraft materials has not been seen.

dashboard_hooks.why: Only data PSI holds; shows campaign structure (2019 round, 2020-21 round), fuel and size coverage.
Core fire-safety message (21% extinguishes, >=26.5% steady); requires per-test data not in PSI.
Places the three NASA cabin atmospheres (101.4/70.3/56.5 kPa) on the tested range.
How BRE links to cone-calorimeter material properties (e.g. PMMA, nylon).

gaps: No Science Documents, Reports, Presentations, Analyzed/Raw Data in PSI: only the experimental table CSV and a metadata zip. All results come from the PSI record text and external sources.
Per-test pressure, flow rate, fuel mole fraction, burn duration and outcome are not in PSI (table notes say pressures are not identified). Pressure ranges are from the dissertation and Wright thesis.

Abstracts of the 11 Elsevier papers in the record (Combustion and Flame, Proc. Combust. Inst., Fire Safety Journal) were not reachable: Crossref has no abstracts, Semantic Scholar elides them, ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403. Only the abstracts of 10.1002/fam.2896 and 10.1177/0734904113495650 (Crossref) and 10.1134/S0010508220040036 (reconstructed from OpenAlex's word index) were read. 10.3850/978-981-07-5936-0_03-01 was not tried.

Update (publication review, data/publications/PSI-20.json): the statement above is partly outdated. A Semantic Scholar batch query returned abstracts for 10.1016/j.combustflame.2021.01.035, 10.1016/j.proci.2020.06.110, 10.1016/j.combustflame.2019.09.030, 10.1016/j.proci.2018.05.006 and 10.1016/j.combustflame.2018.01.044, and the Lund University portal gave the abstract of 10.1016/j.firesaf.2019.02.003. The Dehghani 2021 abstract confirms the dissertation-based findings (59 tests, 21-40% O2, 0.56-1 bar, steady flames at nominal 26% O2 and above, end points above 94% of steady heat flux) and adds that the analysed mixtures had heats of combustion of 23.6 and 47.2 kJ/g. Still unread: 10.1016/j.combustflame.2023.112809, 10.1016/j.proci.2022.08.107, 10.1016/j.combustflame.2021.111572, 10.1016/j.firesaf.2016.11.003, 10.1016/j.combustflame.2015.05.005 and 10.3850/978-981-07-5936-0_03-01 (no abstract anywhere; ScienceDirect accepted manuscripts refuse automated access).

NASA Glenn ACME page in the record (www1.grc.nasa.gov/.../acme/) now redirects to a generic NASA combustion-science page with no BRE content. Used instead: science.nasa.gov ACME and BRE pages, a 2021 NASA JASMAC-33 presentation (NTRS 20210022542), the 2015 Researcher's Guide to Combustion Science (pre-flight description only), NTRS 20160010073/20170009141 (drop-tower precursor), and UMD theses (Dehghani 2022, Wright 2021) not listed in the PSI record.

Dissertation quotes come from the PDF's text layer, in which equations and symbols are garbled. The physics.equations taken from it (heat-of-gasification balance, effective B number, flame height, flame temperature, X_r fit) were reconstructed from that garbled text and checked for internal consistency; the full definition of the group Omega (Eq. 4.33) and the exponent of the later power-law X_r fit could not be read.
Count mismatch: PSI table sums to 194 flames ignited; dissertation reports 149 successful ignitions (round 1 analysis used 59). Not resolved.
Oxygen threshold wording differs: researchImpacts says 21% flames self-extinguished; JASMAC slides say below ~25%; table lists both 25% and 26.5% as nominal levels in different rounds.

Table data issues: '3400%' (2019 Mar 7) and '2100%' (2019 Apr 1) are spreadsheet percent-format artefacts, read as 34 and 21; 2020 Dec 4 row is listed after Dec 5; 2019 Apr 1 had 0 flames ignited (reason not given).
The evidence.parquet text chunk for the table is truncated after row 5 although it reports 19 non-empty rows; table statistics here were computed from the CSV.
Metadata zip is named 'PSI-20_metadata_PSI-96_ACME BRE.zip' (refers to PSI-96); its contents are PSI-20. Record field totalFileSize (~2.04 TB) does not match the two files (~16 kB) listed.
Investigator roles differ: PSI lists Sunderland as Project Scientist; UMD and NASA describe him as Co-Investigator.
PSI record says 16 publications; 15 have DOIs; the Bustamante MS thesis has a DRUM link only in the metadata zip. ACME project count differs between sources (five vs six experiments).
No text addressed to an AI or unrelated instructions was found in the PSI files.

Source quality: several key results (O2 threshold, burn durations, material mapping, extinction-time scaling) rest on a PhD dissertation (Dehghani 2022), a master's thesis (Wright 2021) and a conference slide deck (JASMAC-33, 2021) rather than on the peer-reviewed papers, whose abstracts could not be read (see above).
